note: Narration templates for the guided tours. Figures come from {placeholders} filled from the live data; conclusions are chosen by rules in the app ({"by": fact, "cases": {...}}). The weekly tour agent may refine wording and choose examples, within the rules checked by tools/validate.py.

gap.title: Is AI shrinking the gap from research to change?

intro.say: Each arc is one breakthrough, coloured by where the research began: a university, a government lab or industry. It runs from the start of research to the first product, and a thinner arc continues to mainstream use where that followed.

yes: For example: {exTitle}. Research {exWhere} began in {exR}; the first product came in {exP}
cases.no: Select any arc to see its story.

say: Here is a century of breakthroughs

cases.yes: . Where mainstream use followed, the typical wait after the first product was {adopt} years.

cases.shrunk: Overall, the typical gap from research to first product has shrunk by at least two years: {pre} years for research begun before 1970, against {recent} years for research begun since 2000.
cases.grown: Overall, the typical gap from research to first product has grown by at least two years: {pre} years for research begun before 1970, against {recent} years for research begun since 2000.
cases.flat: Overall, the typical gap from research to first product has changed by no more than two years: {pre} years for research begun before 1970, against {recent} years for research begun since 2000.
cases.unclear: There is not yet enough data to say how the gap from research to first product has changed overall.

say: But much recent research has not yet reached a first product. Counting that unfinished work,

cases.holds: the typical gap for research since 2010 comes to about {kmYears} years, still clearly quicker than for research begun before 1970.
cases.weakens: the typical gap for research since 2010 comes to about {kmYears} years, which is not clearly quicker than for research begun before 1970.
cases.tooEarly: it is too early to be sure.
cases.unclear: there is not yet enough data to tell.

gapchart.say: This chart tracks the typical gap decade by decade, then sketches possible scenarios beyond today, including ones shaped by AI and digital twins.

cases.ai: Since 2000, AI itself has had the shortest typical gap from research to first product, at about {fastestYears} years.
cases.other: Since 2000, {fastestName} has had the shortest typical gap from research to first product; AI ranks {aiRankWord} of {nFields} fields.

say: Select one field, as here with AI, and its sub-fields get their own tracks.

cases.faster: Since 2010, AI-driven work has typically been quicker to reach a first product: {ai} years, against {oth} for the rest.
cases.slower: Since 2010, AI-driven work has typically taken longer to reach a first product: {ai} years, against {oth} for the rest.
cases.similar: Since 2010, AI-driven work has typically taken about as long as the rest to reach a first product: {ai} years against {oth}.
cases.unclear: There are not yet enough AI-driven milestones to compare.

cases.faster: Looking ahead, the estimates suggest AI-assisted work will be quicker: {aiOut} years, against {convOut} for conventional work.
cases.slower: Looking ahead, the estimates suggest AI-assisted work will take longer than conventional work.
cases.similar: Looking ahead, the estimates show little difference between AI-assisted and conventional work.

say: So, is AI shrinking the gap?

cases.0: None of the four measures here points to yes.
cases.1: One of the four measures here points to yes.
cases.2: Two of the four measures here point to yes: exactly half.
cases.3: Three of the four measures here point to yes.
cases.4: All four measures here point to yes.

say: The answer updates as new evidence arrives.

heatchart.say: The heatmap shows how the typical gap from research to first product varies by field and by decade. Since 2010, {fastField} has been quickest and {slowField} slowest.

aichart.say: Each dot is one milestone, and the teal dots are AI-driven. For research since 2010, those typically took about {aiMed} years to reach a first product, against {restMed} for the rest.

horizon.title: What AI-assisted products are on the horizon for the energy system?

intro.say: The government's AI for clean energy vision is divided into several areas. Each diamond marks a story linked to one of those areas, and the stories play through in date order from 1980 onwards.

radar.say: The AI Energy Vision Radar shows how close each area's technologies are to everyday use: {nResearch} in research, {nPilot} in pilots, {nCommercial} in early commercial use and {nScale} widely used. Already in use in Great Britain: {nGB}.

cases.some: The automated search agents have recently found {newCount} new items, including {newTitle}. Mark them as reviewed, and next time you will see only what has arrived since.
cases.none: The automated search agents have found nothing new recently. Mark the radar as reviewed, and next time you will see only what has arrived since.

cases.some: Over the next five years, {nextCount} products are expected. The soonest is {nextTitle}, around {nextYear}, and {busiestArea} has the most on the way.
cases.none: On current data, no products are expected within the next five years.

changes.say: The Forecast drift chart, for clean energy only, tracks when each technology is expected to arrive. Each time the agents revise an estimate, the change appears here, so you can see which forecasts are holding steady and which have moved.

slide.say: For a briefing, the PowerPoint report window creates a single-slide summary, ready to drop into a deck.

say: So, what is on the horizon?

cases.busy: A busy pipeline, and the radar shows which areas are closest to everyday use.
cases.steady: A steady pipeline, and the radar shows which areas are moving towards everyday use.
cases.quiet: Little has appeared in the data so far, so watch the radar as the agents carry on searching.

pipechart.say: The pipeline chart follows each technology from its area, through its readiness, to whether Great Britain has deployed it. So far, {pipeGB} of {pipeTotal} have been deployed there.

intro.say: New technology can give attackers fresh ways in; together these form the attack surface. This filter keeps only technologies that widen it, {attackPct} per cent of everything tracked, from smart grid-edge devices to AI agents.

say: The Cyber lens estimates how long security took to catch up with new technology. Only {secResearched} cases are researched with a source; the rest are rough guides from related milestones.

cases.slow: Typical wait: {lag} years, which is long.
cases.fast: Typical wait: {lag} years, which is quick.

cases.some: Gaps remain. Some technologies that arrived since 2010 still have no security response recorded in their category. They are shown first. So far there are {gapCount}, including {gapTitle}.
cases.none: In this data, no technology that has arrived since 2010 is flagged as an open gap, though many of the responses shown are only rough guides taken from related categories.
cases.proxy: Gaps are hard to judge yet: most technologies here have not had their own security response researched, so the chart shows the nearest related security milestone as a rough guide. The agents are researching them, most recent first.

example.say: This card names a risk and ways to reduce it, linked to recognised guidance: the National Cyber Security Centre's Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF), Ofgem's CAF Overlay, plus NIST guidance from the US, North America's NERC CIP and international IEC 62443.

cases.some: Each week, an AI agent logs newly published security guidance, giving priority to the CAF and to Ofgem's publications. The latest: {guideTitle}.
cases.none: Each week, an AI agent logs newly published security guidance, giving priority to the CAF and to Ofgem's publications.

caution.say: This tour draws on AI-assisted research meant to prompt discussion; it is not security advice. Always involve qualified experts, and your regulator where relevant.

say: So, is security keeping pace?

cases.improving: Security is catching up faster than it used to.
cases.worsening: Security is taking longer to catch up than it used to.
cases.flat: The pace of catching up has barely changed.

secchart.say: This chart shows how many years technologies waited for a security response. Apart from {secResearched} researched cases, bars are rough guides drawn from related milestones, not researched facts. The longest wait shown is {secLongestYears} years, for {secLongestTitle}.

intro.say: Research does not just change products; it can also make fortunes. This chart, Time to a fortune, follows founders from starting a company to the stock market listing, sale or valuation that made them rich.

research.say: Of {nFortunes} fortunes here, {nResearch} began with work in a university or research lab. For those founders, research brought not only new products but also their wealth.

cases.faster: The journey from founding to fortune looks shorter: about {preYears} years for companies founded before 1970, against about {recentYears} years for those founded since 2015. But recent companies still on their way are not counted, which may flatter them.
cases.slower: The journey from founding to fortune is getting longer: about {preYears} years for companies founded before 1970, against about {recentYears} years for those founded since 2015.
cases.similar: The journey from founding to fortune is about as long as ever: roughly {preYears} years for companies founded before 1970, against about {recentYears} years for those founded since 2015. Recent companies still on their way are not counted yet.
cases.unclear: There are not yet enough fortunes from recently founded companies to compare eras.

fastest.say: Sorted by speed, the quickest journey so far comes first: {fastestCo}, which took {fastestTime} to go from founding to fortune.

cases.faster: With the filter set to the UK only, research that began in the UK reached a product in {ukYears} years, faster than the {rowYears} years in the rest of the world.
cases.slower: With the filter set to the UK only, research that began in the UK took {ukYears} years to reach a product, slower than the {rowYears} years in the rest of the world.
cases.similar: With the filter set to the UK only, research that began in the UK reached a product in about the same time as in the rest of the world: {ukYears} years against {rowYears}.
cases.unclear: With the filter set to the UK only, there is not yet enough evidence to say whether UK research reaches a product faster or slower than research elsewhere.

uni.say: Now the filter shows university projects. Those yet to reach a product number {nUni}; any still on their way could become breakthroughs, and perhaps fortunes, in future.

table.say: The Table lists every milestone. Sort by any column, such as the gap between milestones, and select a row to read its story.

say: From lab to fortune:

cases.faster: the journey from founding a company to a fortune looks to be getting shorter, though many recent companies are still on their way.
cases.slower: the journey from founding a company to a fortune is getting longer.
cases.similar: the journey from founding a company to a fortune seems to take about as long as ever.
cases.unclear: it is too early to say whether the journey from founding a company to a fortune is getting shorter or longer.

fortchart.say: Watch the race unfold through time. Each bubble is a fortune, sized by net worth. Gold rings mark founders whose companies grew out of research: {fortResearch} of {fortCount}.

intro.say: This model is kept up to date by AI agents, automated programs that run every week. So far it holds {nMilestones} milestones.

research.say: A research agent searches for new breakthroughs and products across every field of AI, including each area of AI for clean energy. Everything it adds appears in the 'Data changes' view.

qa.say: A second agent checks each new entry independently. It requires more than one source, and the quoted evidence must really appear on the cited page. Nothing is ever deleted.

more.say: Further agents track new security guidance, shown here in the Cyber lens, and keep these walk-throughs up to date. Every change must pass automatic checks before it is published.

say: The 'Data quality' view shows that {pctSourceCited} percent of records now cite a checked source.

cases.scored: Once a forecast's outcome is known, it is scored against what really happened. So far, {fcResolved} forecasts have been scored.
cases.none: Each forecast is recorded now and will be scored against what really happens once the outcome is known.

labels.say: Each record carries a label showing how it was produced and checked: source-cited, AI-compiled or AI estimate. Use the Filters panel to show only the records with the labels you want.

arrange.say: Pick a ready-made view to arrange the panels for exploring, presenting, analysing or an AI for clean energy briefing. Save your own under My views, which are kept in your file. Any view can be shared as a link.

answer.say: Use Help on the toolbar, or any 'i' button, to find out what each feature does. Because AI maintains this model, it may contain errors, so check anything important against the original sources.

whatifchart.say: The What if? chart gives rough estimates, not firm predictions. It shows how much sooner technologies not yet available might arrive if AI speeds up steps such as discovery, simulation and approvals. An agent updates the underlying research weekly.

say: Of {nGap} milestones that have already arrived, {longestTitle} took longest, at {longestYears} years. Among recent arrivals, {quickRecentTitle} was quickest, at about {quickRecentYears} years.
Since 2010, milestones in {fastField} have typically arrived fastest, in about {fastFieldYears} years, and those in {slowField} slowest, in about {slowFieldYears} years.

cases.yes: {improvedField} sped up most, from about {improvedFrom} years in the 1990s to about {improvedTo} years in the 2010s.
cases.no: No field clearly sped up between the 1990s and the 2010s.

cases.similar: Among research-led milestones since 2010, AI-driven work has typically taken about as long to reach a product as the rest: {aiMed} years against {restMed}. This is based on {aiCount} AI-driven milestones, so treat it with caution.
cases.slower: Among research-led milestones since 2010, AI-driven work has typically taken longer to reach a product: {aiMed} years against {restMed}. This is based on {aiCount} AI-driven milestones, so treat it with caution.
cases.unclear: There are not yet enough AI-driven milestones to compare.

say: Of {pipeTotal} clean energy technologies, {pipeResearch} are in research, {pipePilot} piloting, {pipeCommercial} in first commercial use and {pipeScale} at scale; {pipeGB} are deployed in Great Britain.

cases.early: Most are still at an early stage, so proving them at scale is the next challenge.

say: This chart tracks {driftCount} forecasts. The busiest year is {driftPeakYear}, when {driftPeakCount} are expected to arrive.

cases.closed: None is still awaiting a related security milestone, though only {secResearched} matches are researched; the rest are rough proxies.

say: Of {fortCount} fortunes tracked here, {fortResearch} began in a university or research lab. The quickest to be made was {fortFastest}, in {fortFastestTime}.

cases.faster: Recent fortunes have been made faster than earlier ones.
cases.slower: Recent fortunes have taken longer to make than earlier ones.
cases.similar: Recent fortunes have taken about as long to make as earlier ones.
cases.unclear: There are not yet enough recent fortunes to compare them with earlier ones.

whatif.say: In this scenario, the measures in AI for clean energy bring expected technologies forward by about {wiAvg} years on average. By 2030, {wi2030AI} would have arrived, against {wi2030Now} on current trends. The biggest lever is {wiTopLever}. This is an illustration, not a forecast.

say: This week's analysis, updated {updatedAt}.

cases.some: The agents added {newCount} milestones this week, including {newTitles}.
cases.none: No new milestones were added this week, so this is a review of the evidence.

w1.say: Google Project Suncatcher TPU satellite in orbit began as a Google design study of solar-powered AI chips in space. This month a prototype reached orbit, and Google says it booted, ran a prompt and returned a haiku. An early proof, not a fleet.

w2.say: Bepirovirsen: first antisense drug for hepatitis B began as an Ionis drug designed to block the virus's genetic messages, later licensed to GSK. US regulators approved it this month. In final trials, a minority of patients were functionally cured, against none on placebo.

w3.say: Is AI speeding things up? Since 2010, {aiCount} AI-driven milestones typically took {aiMed} years from research to first use, compared with {restMed} for everything else. Treat this as a hint, not proof: AI milestones are fewer and more recent.

w4.say: Security often trails the technology it protects. This week brought new guidance on moving to post-quantum encryption. Across {secCount} milestones, the typical lag is {secMedian} years, and {secOpen} gaps remain open. The longest wait was {secLongestTitle}, at {secLongestYears} years.

w5.say: In AI for clean energy, corrections now record silicon solar cells, utility-scale wind and grid-scale batteries as deployed in Britain. A milestone on dynamic rating of Britain's power lines was also added. Of {pipeTotal} items, {pipeScale} have reached scale and {pipeResearch} remain in research.

w6.say: Size-adjustable pediatric heart valve (Autus) grew from Boston Children's lab work on a valve that expands as a child grows. After a first implant in a young patient and a larger trial, US regulators approved it this month, and Edwards bought the company.

open.say: This is the Gap explorer. Use the tabs at the top to switch charts; your filters apply to all of them. Select a milestone to open its story, and What if? will jump to that same milestone.

gapsort.say: Here the Gap explorer is sorted and zoomed in. You can sort and colour the bars in different ways. Drag across the chart to zoom into a span of years, and double-click to reset the view.

filter.say: The filter bar narrows any chart by search, field or origin; here it shows energy only. With fewer items on screen, each row gets taller and the timeline zooms in to fit.

heat.say: In the heatmap, each cell holds a group of milestones. Select a cell to list them in the side panel, which stays open while you read a story.

ai.say: In AI vs the rest, drag across the chart to draw a box and zoom in. Milestone labels appear once there is room. To list a group of milestones instead, switch to select mode.

pipe.say: The pipeline follows technologies through their stages of development. Select any bar or flow to list the technologies behind it.

drift.say: In Forecast drift, each bar counts the milestones expected to arrive in a given year. Select a bar to list them. Trails show how a milestone's expected date has moved each time its forecast was revised.

sec.say: Security lag shows the wait between a technology and a security response. Open gaps come first; you can also sort by arrival or longest wait. Only {secResearched} responses are researched with a source; the rest are rough guides from related later milestones.

fort.say: Press play to watch the race to a fortune unfold over time, or select a bubble to read that company's story.

whatif.say: What if? shows how arrival dates could shift when practical AI levers are applied. The ambitious scenario is on screen. Switch scenario or adjust the levers, then select a row to see the reasoning and any research behind it.

insight.say: Finally, back on the heatmap, the Insight callout summarises what the chart shows, and can be read aloud with subtitles. Select any number in it to see where it comes from. You can also save any chart as an image or a CSV file.

say: AI for clean energy: this week's analysis, updated {cleanUpdatedAt}.

cases.some: The agents added {cleanNewCount} clean energy technologies this week, including {cleanNewTitles}.
cases.none: No clean energy technologies were added this week, so this is a review of the pipeline.

c1.say: Start with speed. Since 2010, the {aiCount} AI-driven milestones took a median of {aiMed} years to go from research to real use, against {restMed} for the rest. The AI group is small and the evidence is mixed, so treat this as a hint, not proof.

c2.say: The pipeline holds {pipeTotal} clean energy technologies: {pipeResearch} in research, {pipePilot} in pilot, {pipeCommercial} in first commercial use and {pipeScale} at scale. {pipeGB} are used in Great Britain. Checks also scaled back a claim: liquid air storage moved from commercial to pilot.

c3.say: Some ideas did move forward. AI assurance for energy, which is about checking that AI systems used in energy can be trusted, moved from research to pilot this week. Its status in Great Britain also changed from planned to trial.

c4.say: In the what-if scenario, practical AI levers would bring {wi2030AI} clean energy technologies into real use by 2030, against {wi2030Now} expected now. {wiTopLever} is the strongest lever. This is a modelled scenario, not a forecast.

c5.say: Finally, trust. {secOpen} clean energy technologies still have no researched security response, and these open gaps are listed first. A second AI model also disputed a good share of this week's new entries, so those stay flagged until they are checked.

clean-ai.say: We track {cleanAiCount} AI-driven clean energy technologies, listed here. Of these, {cleanAiGB} are already used in Great Britain and {cleanAiResearch} are still in research. Of the AI for clean energy areas on the radar, {cleanAiTopArea} has the most.

cases.some: {cleanNext5GB} of them are already in use or on trial in Great Britain; the rest would be new here.
cases.none: None of them is in use or on trial in Great Britain yet.
